author: Carlos Martinez
title: Anti-Roll Bars and Balance: How ARB Changes Weight Transfer
description: Learn how anti-roll bar stiffness shifts understeer and oversteer. Adjust ARB to dial in the balance your driving style needs.

sections.p: An anti-roll bar (ARB) does one job: resist the chassis roll that happens when a car corners. Stiffer ARB means less body roll. But the real story is what that roll resistance does to tire grip and weight transfer. Change your ARB and you move the car's balance from understeer to oversteer, or the reverse. It is one of the most direct ways to shift how a car behaves mid-corner without touching your setup baseline.

Understanding ARB tuning separates drivers who are guessing from those who are methodical. A quarter-turn adjustment can be the difference between a car that pushes the front into the apex and one that pivots predictably. The mechanism is simple physics, but the effect on your lap time is real.

When you turn the wheel, centripetal force pushes the chassis toward the outside of the corner. The suspension compresses on the outside wheel and extends on the inside wheel. An ARB is a torsional spring connecting the left and right suspension. When one side compresses more than the other, the ARB twists and resists that imbalance.

A stiffer ARB resists roll more aggressively. The chassis stays flatter. A softer ARB allows more roll, and the chassis leans into the corner. This roll does not happen uniformly on both axles. Front roll and rear roll are controlled separately by front and rear ARBs. That separation is where balance tuning happens.

list: Stiffer front ARB: reduces front roll, keeps front tires loaded more evenly, reduces understeer.
Softer front ARB: allows more front roll, concentrates load on the outside front tire, increases understeer.
Stiffer rear ARB: reduces rear roll, keeps rear tires loaded more evenly, reduces oversteer.
Softer rear ARB: allows more rear roll, concentrates load on the outside rear tire, increases oversteer.

sections.tip: ARB changes the moment the car enters the corner. Unlike spring rates, which affect the absolute ride height and compliance over bumps, ARB is purely about how roll resistance shifts grip between inside and outside tires. This makes ARB one of the fastest levers for tuning balance.

sections.p: Understeer means the front tires lose grip before the rear. The car pushes wide at the apex. Oversteer means the rear loses grip first. The tail slides. Your ARB tuning pulls the balance one way or the other.

A common baseline is to tune front and rear ARB to achieve a neutral balance: the car understeers slightly on entry, then pivots mid-corner, and feels neutral on exit. But neutral is a starting point, not a law. Some drivers prefer a car that oversteers slightly because it feels more responsive to steering input. Others prefer a stable, slightly understeering car because it is more forgiving in traffic and over bumps.

To shift the balance toward more oversteer, stiffen the rear ARB or soften the front. To shift toward more understeer, stiffen the front ARB or soften the rear. A one-step change on the rear ARB dial can swing the balance noticeably, especially on high-downforce cars where roll is less pronounced.

sections.h2: Reading your balance and knowing what to change

sections.p: The diagnostic is the lap. You need to identify whether the car is understeering or oversteering at a specific point in the corner, then trace that back to an ARB adjustment.

On corner entry (turn-in), if the car feels like it is fighting the steering input and the nose is not dropping into the line, you have understeer. This usually means the front is rolling excessively and loading up the outside tire too much. Stiffen the front ARB or soften the rear ARB.

Mid-corner (apex), if the rear is sliding and the car feels twitchy or like it might spin, you have oversteer. This usually means the rear is rolling too much or the front is too stiff. Soften the rear ARB or stiffen the front ARB. Soften the rear is the faster tweak if you need immediate response.

On exit, if the car understeers and does not track cleanly off the apex, the front is not loaded. Stiffen the front ARB. If the car oversteers and the rear steps out as you feed in throttle, soften the rear ARB or stiffen the front.

olist: Record a lap and watch the replay. Note the specific corner and phase (entry, mid, exit) where the balance felt wrong.
Identify understeer or oversteer by how the car responded to steering input.
Make one ARB change: stiffen or soften front or rear by one step (usually a 2 to 5 percent change on the dial, depending on the car).
Record another lap at the same car and fuel load. Do not try to drive harder; match your input and speed as closely as possible.
If the change helped, repeat it one more time in the same direction. If it made it worse, reverse the change and try the opposite axle.

sections.tip: Do not chase balance through a whole setup list. Change ARB first, because it is the fastest tuning lever and will give you clear feedback. Only move to springs, bars, or geometry if ARB alone cannot solve the problem.

sections.p: A stiffer ARB keeps tire load more evenly distributed between inside and outside tires during a corner. This means all four tires operate closer to their optimum load and temperature window. A softer ARB concentrates load onto the outside tire, which can cause that tire to overheat while the inside tire stays cool and underutilized.

Over a long stint, tire temperature consistency matters. If your outside front tire is cooking and your inside front tire is cold, the car will feel unstable and inconsistent. A slightly stiffer front ARB can smooth out that temperature spread and improve consistency without making the car feel nervous.

In qualifying or a single-lap shootout, concentrating all the load onto the outside tire can produce one peak-grip moment. That is a valid strategy if you are chasing a single fast lap. Over a race stint, ARB stiffness that keeps tires in a narrower temperature band will be faster.

sections.h2: Setting ARB as part of a baseline

sections.p: A common starting point for most road-racing cars in iRacing is to set front and rear ARB to a moderate position, usually around 50-60 percent on the slider, then tune balance through front and rear wing angle, brake bias, or throttle map before moving to ARB. This gives you a responsive car that is not overly sensitive to small changes.

If you are inheriting a setup or building from scratch, leave ARB in the middle and drive the car as-is for three or four laps. Note where the balance breaks. Then make one targeted ARB change. This method prevents you from chasing multiple variables at once and losing sight of the baseline.

For high-downforce cars (GT3, GTP), ARB changes are smaller in effect because the aero load flattens the chassis. You might need larger swings in ARB to notice a change. For low-downforce cars (formula, roadsters), even a small ARB tweak is obvious.

Fast, high-speed corners demand a stiffer ARB to keep the chassis flat and tires loaded predictably. A soft ARB can feel wallowy and unpredictable at speed. Tracks like Spa or Daytona favor stiffer front ARB.

Technical, low-speed corners with heavy braking favor a softer ARB because the car is not rolling as much anyway. The extra compliance can help traction out of a slow corner. Tracks like Sebring or Monaco benefit from a softer rear ARB to help the rear maintain grip through tight transitions.

Bumpy tracks require care. A very stiff ARB can make the car harsh over curbs and bumps because the ARB forces both suspension sides to resist roll together, which amplifies bumps. A moderate ARB setting with softer springs or a bump stop is usually better on rough pavement. If you find yourself needing a very stiff ARB at a bumpy track, consider whether the problem is actually springs or ride height instead.

sections.tip: When switching tracks, adjust ARB by one or two steps from your baseline and drive three laps to gauge feel. Do not overthink it. Most tracks work well with a front ARB at 60-70 percent and rear at 50-60 percent. Let the car talk to you before tuning further.

faqs.q: Should I change front or rear ARB first if the car understeers?
faqs.a: Stiffen the front ARB first. Front understeer is usually caused by the front rolling and concentrating load on the outside tire. Stiffening the front ARB keeps load distributed more evenly across both front tires, which restores grip. If front understeer persists, soften the rear ARB as a second step to further bias the balance toward the front. Change one thing at a time and record a lap between each change.

faqs.q: Can ARB alone fix balance, or do I need to adjust suspension geometry too?
faqs.a: ARB can fix most balance issues for a given setup and driving style. However, if your car understeers severely even with a very stiff front ARB, the problem might be insufficient front wing angle, too much brake bias bias bias toward the rear, or a geometry issue like too much front camber loss. Start with ARB and wing angle, then explore other areas if the balance still feels wrong after two or three focused tweaks.

faqs.q: How much does ARB affect tire wear?
faqs.a: A very soft ARB concentrates load on the outside tires during cornering, which can accelerate wear on those edges. A stiffer ARB distributes load more evenly, which generally spreads wear across the tire more uniformly and can extend tire life in a race stint. However, the effect is smaller than brake bias or driving smoothness. ARB tuning for balance usually also improves tire longevity as a side benefit.

faqs.q: Is there an ARB setting that works for all cars and tracks?
faqs.a: No. Each car, track, and driver combination will have a different optimal ARB range. A light formula car and a heavy GT3 respond very differently to the same ARB stiffness. A baseline of front ARB around 60-70 percent and rear ARB around 50-60 percent works for many road-racing cars as a starting point, but always adjust based on how the car feels. Bumpy tracks favor slightly softer ARB, while high-speed circuits favor stiffer settings.
